idiom_name: RSpec DSL: has_http_pact_between + new_interaction with pact-ffi
implementation_notes: pact-ruby v2 keeps the RSpec-shaped DSL but moves the engine to pact-ffi: consumer specs are tagged :pact, declare has_http_pact_between 'CONSUMER', 'PROVIDER' (or has_grpc_pact_between / has_message_pact_between), build an interaction with new_interaction.given(...).upon_receiving(...).with_request(...).will_respond_with(...) and execute it against the started mock server, using matchers (match_type_of, match_each, match_regex, match_uuid) and generators (generate_uuid, generate_from_provider_state). Because it implements the V4 specification, HTTP, gRPC and asynchronous message contracts can coexist in one file; the classic v1 DSL still exists but is in maintenance mode.
code_sketch:
RSpec.describe "StoreClient", :pact do
  has_http_pact_between "store-web", "store-service"
  let(:interaction) do
    new_interaction.given("store 42 exists", id: 42)
      .upon_receiving("a request for store 42")
      .with_request(method: :get, path: "/stores/42")
      .will_respond_with(status: 200, body: { id: match_type_of(42) })
  end
  it("fetches the store") { |mock_server|
    interaction.execute { expect(StoreClient.new(mock_server.url).store(42).id).to eq(42) }
  }
end
pitfalls: The mock server is started per example: a client whose base URL is hard-coded instead of taken from mock_server.url silently talks to the real service or fails to connect.
Provider states carry parameters the provider must honour during verification (given('store 42 exists', id: 42)); a state handler that ignores them makes verification pass against the wrong fixture.
Mixing the v1 and the pact/v2 namespace in one project produces contracts from two different engines with different specification levels.

variants.name: pact-ruby v1: classic RSpec DSL with Pact.service_consumer (maintenance mode)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic Ruby realization configures the mock service once in a pact_helper (Pact.service_consumer 'Zoo App' do has_pact_with 'Animal Service' do mock_service :animal_service do port 1234 end end end), declares interactions inside RSpec examples tagged :pact with animal_service.given(...).upon_receiving(...).with(method: :get, path: '/alligator').will_respond_with(status: 200, body: ...), and verifies them from the provider with Pact.service_provider ... honours_pact_with 'Zoo App' { pact_uri ... } driven by rake pact:verify. It writes v2 pacts and verifies v3 files using only the v2 matching rules, and the maintainers document it as being in maintenance mode behind the pact-ffi based pact/v2 namespace.
variants.code_sketch:
Pact.service_consumer "Zoo App" do
  has_pact_with "Animal Service" do
    mock_service(:animal_service) { port 1234 }
  end
end
describe AnimalServiceClient, :pact => true do
  it "returns the alligator" do
    animal_service.given("an alligator exists").upon_receiving("a request for an alligator")
      .with(method: :get, path: '/alligator').will_respond_with(status: 200, body: { name: 'Betty' })
    expect(subject.get_alligator).to eq(Alligator.new('Betty'))
  end
end
pitfalls: The mock service binds a fixed port (1234 in the documented example), so parallel test processes collide unless the port is centralised or randomised.
Only v2 matching rules (like, term) are honoured, so contracts using newer matcher features verify as if those fields were unconstrained.
Provider verification runs through rake pact:verify with PACT_DESCRIPTION/PACT_PROVIDER_STATE selectors; a state callback that does not reset data between interactions makes failures order-dependent.
